evidence_quotes.quote: Process evaluation data were collected through review of key documentation, quantitative surveys, direct observations, and semi-structured interviews with staff from implementing NGOs and community members.
The study is a cluster-randomised trial conducted in 100 villages in seven blocks of Puri district in the State of Orissa, India.
Figure 1 Latrine construction progress from baseline and over intervention period among intervention villages and control villages (n = 4699 households in March 2012 and n = 4585 in March 2013).
The percentage of households with a latrine (completed or under construction) increased from 8% at baseline to 66% one year after the start of the intervention in March 2012.
TSC subsidies were provided to all households instead of BPL card owners and ‘poor’ households only.

Fifth, activities had to be interrupted for two months as part of the code of conduct governing elections and political unrest in four of the intervention villages prevented any construction activities whatsoever.

country.comment: Conducted in 100 rural villages across seven blocks of Puri district in the State of Orissa, India.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF p. 3, Results — Study setting

effect_estimate.comment: Note: p-value for motivator home visit in past month is reported as p = 0.02 in text on PDF p. 7 and p = 0.05 in Table 4 on PDF p. 11. Health trial outcomes are reported elsewhere; this paper evaluates implementation fidelity, mobilisation awareness, and village latrine coverage.
effect_estimate.value: In the 50 intervention villages, household latrine ownership (completed or under construction) rose from 8% at baseline (October 2010) to 66% in March 2012 (68% among BPL vs 61% among APL households; range 54%–76% across NGOs), while completed latrine coverage rose from 8% to 51% between January 2011 and January 2012 (below the 90% target). Compared with control households, intervention households (n = 807; 408 intervention, 399 control) had higher awareness of the Total Sanitation Campaign (91% vs 49%, p < 0.001), VWSCs (51% vs 9%, p < 0.001), adolescent girls groups (23% vs 8%, p < 0.01), wall paintings (44% vs 7%, p < 0.001), and sanitation home visits in the past 3 months (65% vs 3%, p < 0.001), whereas recall of participatory mapping/transect walks (6% vs 10%, p = 0.04) and wealth ranking (0% vs 1%, p = 0.09) was negligible. In village-level linear regressions across the 50 intervention villages (Table 4), March 2012 latrine coverage was positively associated with seeing wall paintings (beta = 0.171, 95% CI: 0.001 to 0.341, p = 0.05), receiving a village motivator visit in the past month (beta = 0.216, 95% CI: -0.000 to 0.431, p = 0.05 in Table 4; p = 0.02 in text), and holding >=5 VWSC meetings (beta = 0.178, 95% CI: 0.010 to 0.346, p = 0.04), but not with other mobilisation indicators; process documentation showed that BPL-only subsidy targeting provoked community tensions, prompting implementers to extend subsidies to all households.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 4, Fidelity assessment — Latrine construction; PDF p. 7–11, Exposure to intervention, Discussion, and Tables 2 & 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods study appraised with MMAT (design ceiling = 2). Directly observes and documents administrative/institutional implementation mechanisms on the ground over 14+ months (BPL card verification, wealth-ranking tensions leading implementers to extend subsidies to all households, household co-contribution registers and complaints after the subsidy increase from INR 2,200 to INR 3,200, VWSC functioning, NGO motivator household visits, and two-month election code-of-conduct suspension) alongside observed household latrine construction.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 2–7, Methods & Results; PDF p. 9–11, Discussion & Table 4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines BPL card / Gram Panchayat list eligibility for TSC subsidies (ELIGIBILITY, documentation), wealth-ranking identification of poor non-BPL households and discretionary extension of subsidies to all households to avert community tensions (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, hardship_exception, discretion), subsidy levels (INR 2,200 raised to INR 3,200) and matching household material/labour co-contributions (BURDEN, fees), community complaints/disputes over subsidy increases and sand prices (complaint), participatory governance via VWSCs, PRA, and Kumari committees (participation), NGO village motivator door-to-door construction/logistics support (bureaucratic_assistance), NGO–Gram Panchayat coordination and political unrest/election code-of-conduct halts (political_coordination, delay).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Although conducted alongside a 100-village cluster-randomised controlled trial (whose trial protocol/health impact design is reported elsewhere), this study itself is a mixed-methods process evaluation combining qualitative primary components (semi-structured interviews with NGO staff/motivators and community members, review of NGO/VWSC records) and quantitative primary components (longitudinal direct latrine observations, cross-sectional surveys of 807 households and 170 VWSC members, and observational village-level linear regressions within the 50 intervention villages).

study_design.value: Mixed-methods process evaluation conducted in connection with a cluster-randomised controlled trial (document review, semi-structured interviews, longitudinal direct observations of latrine construction every 6–8 weeks, and cross-sectional household and VWSC member surveys with village-level t-tests and linear regression)
